slides.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
slides.say: This deck follows the chapter's own concept taxonomy: ninety concepts in six branches, of which forty-two carry a worked example. The worked examples are re-run by the build under the interpreter named in each console caption, and the deck is refused if one stops agreeing. Figures that come from outside that run say Recorded or NOT EXECUTED on their own slide. The text is Mastering Bitcoin, third edition, chapter 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), free under CC BY-SA 4.0.
slides.concept: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Six parts. The stories carry the why, the programs carry the proof, and every slide number on this list is printed bottom-right as we pass it. A question to think about is this: which part do you expect to be hardest? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in every section.
slides.concept: Six parts, one route - and every claim arrives with its receipt

slides.title: The outcomes this session serves
slides.say: The branches are the chapter's own: Money, Network, Wallet, Usage, Foundations, Nature. Say at the start that the order of the lecture is the order of the taxonomy, so that a student who opens the interactive page afterwards finds the same tree.
slides.concept: One outcome, one chapter, every concept on the page

slides.title: One chapter, six branches
slides.say: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Money, Network, Wallet, Usage, Foundations and Nature.
slides.concept: Six branches - every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Origins
slides.say: Three stories explain why Bitcoin looks the way it does: a newspaper headline carved into the first block, the first purchase made with bitcoin, and forty years of failed attempts at digital money. Each story is dated and sourced on its own slide.
slides.concept: Three stories that explain why Bitcoin looks the way it does

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 3 January 2009. The first Bitcoin block ever mined carries a piece of that morning's newspaper: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'. It proves the block could not have been made earlier than that headline, and at the same time records why the system was built - in the middle of a banking crisis, by someone who wanted money that needs no bailout and no bank. The source is Bitcoin genesis block coinbase text, block 0, 2009-01-03; The Times front page of 3 January 2009; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin (genesis block).
slides.concept: History is written into the chain itself

read.label: Genesis block coinbase, with the headline (tx)

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.say: This is a true story, dated January 2009. Nine days after the genesis block, Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 bitcoin to Hal Finney, a veteran cryptographer who had answered the whitepaper with curiosity instead of dismissal and famously tweeted 'Running bitcoin'. Finney had worked on PGP and had built the first reusable proof-of-work system years before Bitcoin existed - the first payment went to someone who had spent a career preparing for it. The source is Bitcoin block 170, 2009-01-12, the first bitcoin transaction (Satoshi Nakamoto to Hal Finney, 10 BTC); Hal Finney, 'Running bitcoin', twitter.com/halfin, 2009-01-10.
slides.concept: Peer to peer meant person to person from day one

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.say: Bitcoin was not the first attempt at digital money. David Chaum's blind-signature ecash of the 1980s ended with the bankruptcy of his company DigiCash, and Adam Back's Hashcash of 1997 priced email spam with proof of work. Wei Dai's b-money and Nick Szabo's bit gold, both of 1998, were never built because neither could agree on a history without a leader. The sources are Nakamoto's 2008 paper and the original text of each author.
slides.concept: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money
slides.say: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Money.
slides.concept: What the currency is, who issues it, and on what schedule

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.say: On the island of Yap, wealth was held in rai, limestone discs up to four metres wide and far too heavy to move. When a stone changed owners it stayed where it lay, and only the community's shared memory of who owned it changed. That is a ledger without a bank, the idea Bitcoin rebuilds. The sources are Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910), and Milton Friedman's Hoover working paper of 1991 with the same title.
slides.concept: Money is a ledger; Bitcoin makes it digital

read.label: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.say: Money has changed form many times: grain-ledger entries in Mesopotamia, the first struck coins in Lydia around 600 BCE, paper notes in Song-dynasty China, and goldsmiths' receipts that became bank money. In 1971 the dollar's last tie to gold was cut, leaving pure fiat money. Bitcoin is the next step in that sequence, money that exists only as digital records. The sources are standard monetary histories and chapter 1 of Mastering Bitcoin, third edition.
slides.concept: Each era changed the ledger-keeper; Bitcoin removed the position

slides.title: Traditional, digital, crypto - side by side
slides.say: The table compares traditional cash, digital money held at banks and cryptocurrency on who issues it, where it exists and who keeps the ledger. The remaining rows ask what sets the supply and how a payment settles. Read down a column to see one kind of money, and across a row to see which property changes. The difference in who keeps the ledger is the subject of this course.
slides.concept: Same uses, different ledgers - and that difference is this course

slides.title: Physical cash: superb in person, stuck there
slides.say: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: which of these failures did cards fix? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Money.
slides.concept: Cash is a bearer instrument: perfect in person, useless on a network

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 1998 - 2002. The web could sell before it could pay: cards were unsafe to type and banks had no internet rails. Confinity, founded 1998 by Max Levchin and Peter Thiel, and X.com, founded 1999 by Elon Musk, raced to fix it, merged in 2000, and became PayPal - sold to eBay for 1.5 billion dollars in 2002. The source is en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal (Confinity 1998, X.com 1999, merger 2000, eBay acquisition 2002); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooz.com and /wiki/Beenz.com (both closed 2001 in the dot-com crash).
slides.concept: Payments went online in 1998-2002; cash never did

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2007 - 2022. Money fails people in documented ways. Kenya, 2007: most adults had no bank, so Safaricom's M-Pesa turned phone credit into the country's money rail. The source is en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Pesa (Safaricom, 2007); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012-2013_Cypriot_financial_crisis (deposit levy, March 2013); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis (2015 capital controls, 60-euro limit); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Venezuela (over 1,000,000% in 2018); CNBC 2022-03-02 and Fortune 2022-03-26 on Ukraine's official crypto donations (Alex Bornyakov, 35 million dollars within the first week).
slides.concept: Crisis or war, banked or not - the need is documented, not theoretical

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.say: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why does the same problem not exist for paper cash? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Double spend.
slides.concept: Perfect copies made digital cash impossible without a referee

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.say: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: what stops the network agreeing on the WRONG order? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Double spend and Consensus.
slides.concept: The referee is everyone, and the whistle is arithmetic

slides.title: One bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis
slides.say: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi. A question to think about is this: how many satoshis buy a coffee at today's price? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Unit.
slides.concept: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: 21 million, by rule - not by promise
slides.say: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why does the sum stop just short of 21 million? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Supply and Issuance.
slides.concept: Scarcity is enforced by arithmetic every node checks

slides.title: The schedule, executed
slides.say: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Supply and Issuance.
slides.concept: Three one-liners reproduce the whole monetary policy

slides.title: Price is discovered, not declared
slides.say: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin. The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Price.
slides.concept: No one sets the price; everyone does

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 22 May 2010. For Bitcoin's first year and a half, nobody knew what a bitcoin was worth, because nobody had ever bought anything with one. Then Laszlo Hanyecz, a Florida programmer, offered 10,000 BTC on a forum to anyone who would bring him two pizzas - and someone did. The source is Guinness World Records, 'First commercial Bitcoin transaction' (Laszlo Hanyecz, 2010-05-22, 10,000 BTC for two pizzas); bitcointalk.org thread 'Pizza for bitcoins?', May 2010.
slides.concept: Price is discovered the first time someone pays

slides.title: The pizza, repriced every few years
slides.say: Every point is a documented milestone - dollar parity in 2011, the first thousand in 2013, the 2017 and 2021 peaks - and the last one was fetched live from mempool.space and CoinGecko while this deck was built, agreeing within 0.1 percent. A question to think about is this: why does this chart need a log scale? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Price; story companion and PIZZA_VALUE.
slides.concept: From 41 dollars to 854 million - price discovery never stopped

slides.title: Network
slides.say: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader. The chapter describes Bitcoin as a distributed, peer-to-peer system in which there is no central server or point of control, and as a protocol, a peer-to-peer network, and a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Network.
slides.concept: No bank in the middle - and what replaces it

slides.title: A bank in the middle vs. peers
slides.say: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader. The chapter describes Bitcoin as a distributed, peer-to-peer system in which there is no central server or point of control, and as a protocol, a peer-to-peer network, and a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: what breaks first in each picture if one machine lies? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Network and Consensus.
slides.concept: Remove the hub and the rules must move to every node

slides.title: Peers find each other without a directory
slides.say: One peer starts out knowing two neighbours, and in each round it asks the peers it has just found for their neighbours. The program counts the rounds of gossip until all seven peers are known, and it reports four. No server or registry is involved, which is why the network needs no directory.
slides.concept: The network is just nodes agreeing to speak alike

slides.title: Rules, not rulers, decide validity
slides.say: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Consensus.
slides.concept: Validity is computed, never decreed

slides.title: Mining pays for honesty
slides.say: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Consensus and History.
slides.concept: Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin

slides.title: Wallets and first use
slides.say: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Wallet and Usage.
slides.concept: Choosing software, holding keys, and the first payment

slides.title: The wallet branch, mapped
slides.say: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Wallet.
slides.concept: A wallet is software for keys, not a bag of coins

slides.title: Your key is your deed - and you may never show it
slides.say: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. Think about this case: your house has a registry if the key is lost. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Key control.
slides.concept: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Who holds the keys, holds the coins
slides.say: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. A question to think about is this: which side was the exchange that lost its customers' coins on? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Key control, Wallet platform and Backup.
slides.concept: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: Mt. Gox: the exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.say: The exchange Mt Gox of Tokyo, led by Mark Karpeles, was once the largest bitcoin exchange in the world. In February 2014 it halted withdrawals, filed for bankruptcy and admitted that about 850,000 bitcoins were gone. Customers had balances on a website, but the keys, and therefore the coins, had been in someone else's hands all along. The figure comes from the Tokyo District Court filing of 28 February 2014 and is reported here, not recomputed.
slides.concept: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins - exchanges included

slides.title: From a phrase to a key, slowly on purpose
slides.say: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong. It begins with the chapter's account of Alice's first start-up, when her noncustodial wallet produces a recovery code that can be used to restore it, and it goes on to the additional data that a recovery code does not contain, and to the payments that some technologies keep outside the public blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Backup and Key control.
slides.concept: Slowness here is a feature priced against attackers

slides.title: Alice's first bitcoin, step by step
slides.say: The Acquisition section lists the ways in which a newcomer obtains a first bitcoin, which is the practical problem a reader faces as soon as the wallet is installed. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Acquisition, Address and Transfer.
slides.concept: Five minutes of app taps hide all of this machinery

slides.title: Foundations
slides.say: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Foundations.
slides.concept: The two old problems Bitcoin finally joined up

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.say: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Foundations and Cryptography.
slides.concept: Bitcoin's novelty is the combination, not the parts

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.say: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Chain and Cryptography.
slides.concept: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.title: A chain that notices tampering
slides.say: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Chain.
slides.concept: History becomes expensive to rewrite, cheap to verify

slides.title: The toolbox under the hood
slides.say: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it. It covers the internet and the rules that computers follow on it, the way programs talk to each other through interfaces, the way data is named and stored, the operating systems and browsers in which wallets live, and the units in which computers count. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Computing and Threats.
slides.concept: Every term here gets its own page section

slides.title: What kind of thing is Bitcoin?
slides.say: The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Nature, Characteristic and Architecture.
slides.concept: Each adjective is engineered, not advertised

slides.title: Beyond the base layer
slides.say: The Transfer section explains what happens when Joe sends bitcoin to Alice. It follows the payment from the moment he presses Send to the moment it is confirmed in a block, and it introduces the objects and ideas involved: the transaction, its inputs and outputs, the fee, the confirmation, the irreversibility, and the newer payments that never reach the public chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Transfer and Semantic bridge.
slides.concept: The chain settles; the edges scale

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.say: Six lines, one per part. If any of them still feels like a claim rather than a fact, the agenda slide names the slides that prove it - and the course page carries the full text. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend to a sceptic first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in every section.
slides.concept: If a line feels unproven, its part's slides carry the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything on this slide is free. The whitepaper is nine pages - read it this week; the textbook is the one this course follows, free under CC BY-SA in the same repository our materials pin. A question to think about is this: who can find today's newest block on mempool.space before the break ends? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1, in Standards and History.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.say: These are the claims you should now be able to make: what a bitcoin is and how far it divides, why twenty-one million is arithmetic and not a promise, and what replaces the bank in the middle. Each claim is proved in a later chapter, and the last box on the slide names the chapter that opens each branch we drew. If you cannot yet say one of them in your own words, return to its branch.
slides.concept: And where each claim gets its proof
